extracted.intended_audience: inventors, startups, and IP professionals considering patent filing or conducting patentability/FTO searches
extracted.subtask_description: A practical guide to performing prior art searches to assess novelty, inventive step, and freedom-to-operate using official patent databases and good search methodology. Covers when to search, which databases to use, search construction, examiner criteria, common mistakes, post-grant monitoring, and when to hire professionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art is any public information that existed before your patent’s filing date including patents, publications, products, or public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed: published patents and patent applications, scientific articles, theses, standards, websites, videos, manuals, public talks, commercial products or public demonstrations. If it was publicly accessible it can count as prior art regardless of language or country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of a prior art search
rubrics_metrics.description: To check if your invention is new and inventive before filing a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal and strategic goals: determine patentability (novelty/non-obviousness), save filing costs, improve application drafting, guide R&D by identifying white spaces, and avoid infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to perform a prior art search
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct searches at several stages: before filing, during prosecution, before product launch, before acquisition/licensing, and post-grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideally done before filing to evaluate novelty; during prosecution to respond to rejections; before product launch for FTO; before acquisition/licensing to verify validity/scope; and post-grant to monitor threats and opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of prior art searches — Novelty search
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelty search determines if your invention is new before you file a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to assess whether any single prior art reference discloses all features of a claim; start here if primary goal is getting a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of prior art searches — Freedom-to-Operate (FTO) search
rubrics_metrics.description: An FTO search ensures your product can be made or sold without infringing others’ patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus is on whether practicing the product would fall within the claims of existing, in-force patents in jurisdictions of interest; differs from novelty search whose goal is patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of prior art searches — Invalidity / Opposition search
rubrics_metrics.description: An invalidity (or opposition) search finds earlier disclosures that could invalidate an existing patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target earlier prior art that anticipates or renders obvious the claims of the asserted patent; important for challenges and litigation strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of prior art searches — State-of-the-art search
rubrics_metrics.description: A state-of-the-art search reviews existing technologies in a field for R&D or competitive intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad landscape review to identify trends, white spaces, and competitor activity rather than testing a single claim for novelty or infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to search — official patent databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use free government databases maintained by major patent offices (USPTO Patent Public Search, Espacenet, WIPO PATENTSCOPE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These databases provide full-text patents/applications, classification and citation data, and field/Boolean search options. Run searches in at least two major sources (e.g., USPTO + WIPO or EPO + JPO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use CPC/IPC classifications alongside keywords
rubrics_metrics.description: CPC/IPC classifications group inventions into categories to find related technologies that keyword searches may miss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify relevant classification codes (chemical processes, medical devices, software methods, etc.) via USPTO/EPO classification search pages and combine classification filters with keywords for precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define the invention clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Break your invention into its essential technical features: purpose, components, and unique aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start by explicitly listing the invention’s core elements so you can target searches to each element and combinations of elements (claims-level thinking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify keywords and synonyms
rubrics_metrics.description: List synonyms, broader and narrower terms relevant to the invention and relevant CPC/IPC codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include alternative terminology, technical jargon, lay terms, and translations where appropriate to capture non-standard disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build effective search queries (Boolean and field tags)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Boolean operators (AND, OR, NOT) and field tags (title, abstract, claims) to construct precise queries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use AND to combine keywords and narrow results, OR to include synonyms, NOT to exclude irrelevant topics, and field tags to search within specific parts of documents. Combine keyword searches with classification filters for best results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search across multiple databases
rubrics_metrics.description: No single database covers everything; run searches in at least two major sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix USPTO, Espacenet, WIPO PATENTSCOPE, and where relevant national databases or commercial services to capture regional/non-English publications and different coverage sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze and document findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Review abstracts and claims first; note publication numbers, filing dates, and applicants, and keep a record of search terms and databases used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documenting search queries, dates, and results supports reproducibility, prosecution strategy, and later defenses. Prioritize reading claims and filing/publication dates to assess relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: What patent examiners check — Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners assess whether all features of a claim appear in a single prior art reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During searches prioritize finding single references that disclose the full claimed combination; partial overlaps may relate to inventive step analysis instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: What patent examiners check — Inventive step / Obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners ask whether combining known elements would have been obvious to a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider plausible combinations of references and whether those combinations render the claim obvious; anticipate obviousness-type rejections when evaluating patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: What patent examiners check — Enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners consider whether the prior art sufficiently describes how to make or use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior disclosure that merely mentions a feature may be less decisive than one that enables practice of the invention; assess level-of-detail in candidate prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common mistakes to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical errors include searching only in English, relying on a single keyword or database, ignoring non-patent literature, failing to check dates carefully, and misinterpreting 'patent pending'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong search is broad enough to uncover global results and narrow enough to focus on truly relevant disclosures. Translate terms, include non-patent literature, and verify publication and priority dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-grant searches and monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: After filing or grant, searches help identify new filings, infringements, competitor continuations, expired patents, and post-grant proceeding windows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In FTO/validity contexts focus on claims of existing patents, monitor recent applications in your space, watch for expirations that open opportunities, and note deadlines for post-grant actions (e.g., U.S. post-grant review windows).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal scope of searches
rubrics_metrics.description: How far back should you search? At least 20 years is recommended, but older publications may still be relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use project-specific judgment: core technologies may have relevant prior art older than 20 years; document decisions on temporal cutoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: International nature of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art is global: a disclosure anywhere in the world can affect your U.S. or European application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search non-U.S. databases and non-English sources; consider translations or professional help to capture foreign-language disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to seek professional help
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent attorneys and professional searchers use advanced commercial tools and provide legal opinions; consider hiring them for core inventions or international filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional tools (Derwent Innovation, Orbit, PatBase) can interpret claims and equivalents more accurately, access non-English full-text, and deliver structured reports. Use professionals when the invention is commercially important or when an FTO/validity opinion is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of weak or incomplete searches
rubrics_metrics.description: A weak or incomplete search may lead to patent rejection or inadvertent infringement of existing patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest sufficient time and breadth in searches to reduce legal and commercial risk; escalate to professionals when uncertain.
